text:
Alexandre Carrier's goal at 13:12 of the third period was the kind that breaks a game open and a model's heart at once. It came on a 1 percent chance, a wrist shot that stretched Montreal's lead to 3-1 and, by the numbers, shouldn't have happened. Toronto was the team that deserved to win this one, taking 55 percent of simulated replays of every shot, and it lost 3-2 anyway.

The data supports the case that the Maple Leafs played the better game. Even-strength expected goals were close (MTL 1.91, TOR 1.82), and the total tilted toward Montreal only through the third, where the numbers don't add up the way the standings do. William Nylander scored twice, the first at 00:48 of the opening period on a 4 percent look and the second at 15:46 of the third to cut the lead to one. He put five shots on goal. Josh Anderson tied it at 10:53 of the first with a bat-in goal, and Zachary Bolduc made it 2-1 at 4:52 of the second.

Goaltending quietly mattered. Jakub Dobes stopped 26 of 28 and saved 0.57 goals above expected, including a 24 percent chance from John Tavares in the third. Sergei Bobrovsky saved 21 of 24 and finished 0.71 below expected. Montreal also won 32 of 53 faceoffs and took the puck away seven times to Toronto's two. Neither team scored on the power play, with Toronto going 0 for 3 and Montreal 0 for 2.
